Chapter 9: Sustaining Momentum—Habits, Reflection, and Course Correction
You know, designing a well-lived life isn’t just a one-and-done kind of project—it's really an ongoing practice. Keeping that momentum going? That means building habits that help you reflect, learn, and stay adaptable along the way.
One habit that makes a huge difference is checking in with your internal compass on a regular basis. Maybe that’s weekly, monthly, or even just every few months. The point is to carve out time to really ask yourself—am I actually moving toward what matters most to me? Where do I feel energized, and where do I feel drained? And what small tweaks could make my days feel more fulfilling?
Sometimes, it’s as simple as jotting down your thoughts in a journal, having a heart-to-heart with a mentor, or taking a quiet walk to let your mind wander. These moments help you surface insights and keep your life on track.
Here’s something to pay attention to: the reflection habit. Give yourself regular chances to pause, review how things are going, and recalibrate your direction if you need to.
But it’s not just about reflecting—celebrating your progress along the way really matters too. Even the small wins deserve some recognition. Think about the steps you’ve taken, the risks you’ve tried, and the things you’ve learned. Each one builds your confidence and motivation to keep moving forward.
So, try to celebrate those small wins. Every little step counts, and when you acknowledge them, you’re reinforcing your own sense of growth and agency.
And let’s be honest—course correction is just part of the journey. Life changes, right? Your values, interests, and circumstances can shift over time. Instead of stubbornly sticking to old goals, the design approach invites you to stay flexible, adjusting your plans as needed.
Here’s a real-world example: imagine you’ve spent a year in a new job and suddenly realize your priorities have changed. Instead of feeling trapped, you can check your compass, brainstorm some new options, and start prototyping again. It’s all about treating your life as a series of experiments—always open to learning and change.
That’s what we mean by iterative design.
When you build reflection and adaptation into your routine, you set up a self-sustaining process for growth. The journey becomes less about chasing some final destination, and more about ongoing discovery—always learning, always evolving.
